mainTopic: The burglar (בא במחתרת) and the רודף: when they may be killed, and whether a warning is needed
overview: This amud is about the burglar who breaks into a house (בא במחתרת) and about the רודף, someone chasing another person to kill him. First the גמרא settles a contradiction: a father breaking into his son's house may not be killed, but a son breaking into his father's house may be. רב adds that he would kill any burglar except רב חנינא בר שילא, who loves him like a father loves a son. A ברייתא teaches that the burglar rules apply on שבת too, and רב ששת explains that we must even dig out a protected burglar from rubble on שבת. Another ברייתא teaches that anyone may kill the burglar, by any method. The גמרא explains why this could not be learned from רוצח, using the rule that two verses which come as one do not teach other cases. Two ברייתות agree that the burglar law applies anywhere on the property, but disagree about the word מחתרת: one says it is just the common case, and the other says breaking in is his warning (התראה). Finally, רב הונא rules that even a קטן who is a רודף may be killed, since a רודף needs no warning. The גמרא defends him against challenges and attempted proofs, ending with two answers that keep his ruling standing.

steps.title: Father breaking in versus son breaking in
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction between two ברייתות by saying one is about a father breaking into his son's home and the other is about a son breaking into his father's home.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, the ruling is about a father breaking in on his son. There, the ruling is about a son breaking in on his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering a contradiction from just before this point. One ברייתא forbids killing a burglar when you are unsure of his intentions, and another allows it, so the גמרא explains that each is talking about a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A father loves his son deeply, so we assume he would not kill his son. Because of that, the son may not kill his father unless he knows for sure the father means to kill. A son has less of that love, so the father may kill the son unless he knows for sure the son would never kill him.

keyTerms.meaning: Here... there; one source is about this case, the other source is about that case
A break-in; a burglar who tunnels or breaks into a house
A father coming in against his son

steps.whatToRemember: The rule for an unclear burglar depends on how much love we can assume the burglar has for the homeowner. A father is assumed not to kill his son; a son is not given that assumption.

phrases.english: Here, it is about a father breaking in on his son,
phrases.notes: This 'here' is the ברייתא that says you may NOT kill the burglar when unsure.

phrases.english: there, it is about a son breaking in on his father.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּאן – בְּאָב עַל הַבֵּן, כָּאן – בְּבֵן עַל הָאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between two ברייתות raised on the previous עמוד
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source is talking about a different situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to give opposite rulings about the same unclear burglar.
steps.terutzMaskana: One ברייתא is about a father breaking in, where killing is forbidden. The other is about a son breaking in, where killing is permitted.

steps.title: רב would kill any burglar except one man
steps.stepSummary: רב says he would kill anyone who broke into his home, except רב חנינא בר שילא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Anyone who breaks into my house, I would kill him, except for רב חנינא בר שילא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a personal example of the burglar law. He would treat every burglar as dangerous, with one exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a burglar is assumed to be ready to kill the homeowner, so the homeowner may kill him first. רב names one person he would not assume that about. The גמרא will now ask why.

keyTerms.meaning: I would kill him
Except for

phrases.english: Rav said:
Anyone who comes in on me through a break-in,
I would kill him,
except for Rav Chanina bar Sheila.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: כֹּל דְּאָתֵי עֲלַאי בְּמַחְתַּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of the love principle from step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב would kill any burglar in self-defense, except רב חנינא בר שילא.

steps.title: Why the exception?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב made an exception for רב חנינא בר שילא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב would not kill רב חנינא בר שילא. This question sets up the next two moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule is that any burglar may be killed. The גמרא wants to know what makes this person different.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רב's exception
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב would not kill רב חנינא בר שילא if he broke in

steps.title: Not because he is righteous
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the reason is that רב חנינא is a צדיק, then rejects that, because a man breaking into a house is not acting like a צדיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is because he is a righteous man, but he is breaking in!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one answer, that he is a צדיק, and immediately knocks it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case he is actually breaking in, so his being a צדיק cannot be the reason. A צדיק does not commit burglary. A different reason is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggested answer that will be rejected)
A righteous person
But look, here

phrases.english: If you say it is because he is a righteous man,
but he is coming in through a break-in!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא מִשּׁוּם דְּצַדִּיק הוּא – הָא קָאָתֵי בְּמַחְתַּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers and rejects a first answer to the question in step 3
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the suggested reason that he is a צדיק
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: His breaking in shows he is not acting like a צדיק, so that cannot be what protects him.

steps.title: He loves me like a father loves a son
steps.stepSummary: The real reason is that רב is sure רב חנינא loves him the way a father loves his son, so he would never kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because I am certain about him that he has compassion on me like a father has compassion on a son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real reason for רב's exception. It is the same idea as the father case in step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 taught that a father breaking in is assumed not to kill his son. רב applies the same idea to a close friend he knows loves him like a father. So even while breaking in, this man is not considered dangerous.

keyTerms.meaning: I am certain; it is clear to me
About him; regarding him
Has compassion, loves

steps.whatToRemember: The burglar may be killed only because we assume he is ready to kill. Where it is clear he loves the homeowner, like a father loves a son, that assumption falls away.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because I am certain about him
that he has compassion on me
like a father has compassion on a son.
phrases.notes: This wording comes from a פסוק, תהלים 103:13.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דְּקִים לִי בְּגַוֵּויהּ דִּמְרַחֵם עָלַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 4 with the correct reason
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב is certain רב חנינא loves him like a father loves a son, so he would not kill רב.

steps.title: Both burglar rules apply on weekdays and on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that both 'דמים לו' and 'אין לו דמים' apply on weekdays and on שבת alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'He has blood' applies both on a weekday and on שבת. 'He has no blood' applies both on a weekday and on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the two burglar פסוקים. It says the day of the week makes no difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אין לו דמים' means a burglar who may be killed, and the killer is not guilty. 'דמים לו' means a burglar who may not be killed, so killing him is murder. The ברייתא says both rules stay the same on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: He has blood: killing this burglar counts as murder
He has no blood: the burglar may be killed and the killer is not guilty
Both on a weekday and on שבת

steps.confusionAlert: 'דמים לו' sounds like the burglar has no protection, but it means the opposite: he is protected, and whoever kills him is guilty of murder.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"He has blood"
both on a weekday and on Shabbat,
"He has no blood"
both on a weekday and on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: דָּמִים לוֹ בֵּין בַּחוֹל בֵּין בַּשַּׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: whether the burglar laws change on שבת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both burglar rules, 'דמים לו' and 'אין לו דמים', apply equally on weekdays and on שבת.

steps.title: Why the שבת clause makes sense for 'no blood'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא grants that for 'אין לו דמים' the ברייתא had to mention שבת, because we might have compared the burglar to people executed by בית דין, who are not executed on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is understandable that 'he has no blood' needed to say both weekday and שבת. You might have thought he is like those executed by בית דין, whom we do not kill on שבת. So it teaches us that we do kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first half of a challenge. The גמרא first agrees that one half of the ברייתא makes sense, to set up a question about the other half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית דין does not carry out executions on שבת. Someone might think the burglar is the same, so you could not kill him on שבת. The ברייתא tells us that self-defense against a burglar is allowed even on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: It is understandable (this part makes sense, but...)
It would have entered your mind to say
People executed by the court
It teaches us

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that killing a burglar is not a court punishment. It is self-defense, which is allowed even on שבת.

phrases.english: It is understandable that "he has no blood"
needed to say both on a weekday and on Shabbat,
since it would have entered your mind to say:
it is just like those executed by the court,
whom we do not kill on Shabbat.
So it teaches us that we do kill him.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים בֵּין בַּחוֹל בֵּין בַּשַּׁבָּת אִיצְטְרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains half of the ברייתא from step 6 to prepare a challenge on the other half
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Grants that the שבת clause is needed for 'אין לו דמים', so that the question on 'דמים לו' will stand out.

steps.title: Why mention שבת for 'he has blood'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if we may not kill this burglar even on a weekday, why would we need to be told we cannot kill him on שבת?
steps.simpleTranslation: But 'he has blood' both on a weekday and on שבת? Now, if on a weekday we do not kill him, is it necessary to say we do not kill him on שבת?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges the other half of the ברייתא. Saying 'on שבת too' seems pointless for the burglar who may not be killed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing is easier to allow on a weekday than on שבת. If it is forbidden even on a weekday, it is surely forbidden on שבת. So the words 'בין בשבת' in 'דמים לו' seem to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: But (introduces the difficult half)
Now, if... (opens a 'this is obvious' argument)
Is it necessary to say?

phrases.english: But "he has blood"
both on a weekday and on Shabbat?
Now, if on a weekday we do not kill him,
is it necessary to say so on Shabbat?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דָּמִים לוֹ בֵּין בַּחוֹל בֵּין בַּשַּׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בשלמא challenge started in step 7
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'בין בחול בין בשבת' attached to 'דמים לו' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If killing is forbidden even on a weekday, it is obviously forbidden on שבת, so the ברייתא's extra words seem unnecessary.

steps.title: We must dig the burglar out on שבת
steps.stepSummary: רב שֵׁשֶׁת explains that the ברייתא mentioned שבת to teach that we must break שבת to clear rubble off a burglar.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת says: it is needed only to teach that we must clear the pile of rubble off him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שֵׁשֶׁת answers the question from step 8. The ברייתא mentioned שבת for the burglar we may not kill, to teach that we must even dig him out on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 asked: if we may not kill him even on a weekday, why say anything about שבת? רב שֵׁשֶׁת says the point is not about killing him at all. The point is that we must save him, even if that means breaking שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (introduces the real purpose of a teaching)
To clear away, to dig out (breaking שבת to save a life)
A pile of stones or rubble

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that once a burglar is not a threat, his life is fully protected, and we must save him even on שבת.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet says:
It is needed only
to clear the pile of rubble off him.
phrases.notes: Picture a wall falling on the burglar on שבת. We must dig him out, even though that breaks שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: לָא נִצְרְכָא אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the case a new purpose: saving him, not killing him
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mentioning שבת seemed pointless, since he may not be killed on any day.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that we must break שבת to dig him out from under rubble.

steps.title: Anyone may strike the burglar, in any way
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the פסוק that anyone may strike the burglar, and that he may be killed by any method.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'And is struck' means by any person. 'And dies' means by any kind of death you are able to kill him with.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that explains two words in the פסוק about the burglar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'והכה' teaches who may strike him: not only the homeowner, but anyone. 'ומת' teaches how he may be killed: by whatever method works.

keyTerms.meaning: And is struck
And dies
By any person

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And is struck" — by any person,
"and dies" — by any kind of death
that you are able to kill him with.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on the burglar's פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone may kill the burglar, and by any method.

steps.title: Why 'by any person' was needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא grants that 'by any person' is needed, because the burglar counts as a רודף, so even an outsider may kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted that 'and is struck' by any person was needed. You might have thought that only the homeowner may kill him, because the burglar is sure the homeowner will fight back, since a person does not hold back when his money is at stake. But another person may not. So the ברייתא teaches that he is a pursuer, so even another person may kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a question. First it agrees that the first lesson of the ברייתא makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the פסוק, we might think only the homeowner is in danger, so only he may kill the burglar. The פסוק teaches that the burglar is a רודף, and anyone may stop a רודף. This sets up the coming question about the second lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, this part is fine (sets up a coming question)
You might have thought

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם מַעֲמִיד עַצְמוֹ עַל מָמוֹנוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person does not hold himself back when his money is at stake
A pursuer trying to kill someone; anyone may stop him

phrases.english: Granted, "and is struck" by any person was needed,
because you might have thought:
it is the homeowner whom the burglar is sure about,
phrases.notes: He means: the burglar is sure the homeowner will fight back, so he comes ready to kill him.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאֵין אָדָם מַעֲמִיד עַצְמוֹ עַל מָמוֹנוֹ,
phrases.english: since a person does not hold himself back when his money is at stake,
but another person — no.
So it teaches us
that he is a pursuer,
and so even another person may also kill him.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא ״וְהֻכָּה״ בְּכׇל אָדָם אִיצְטְרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the first half of the ברייתא, to set up a question on the second half
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Agrees that the first lesson is needed, so it can ask about the second lesson.

steps.title: Why do we need 'by any death'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs 'ומת' to teach that any method of killing is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But 'and dies' by any kind of death you are able to kill him with — why do I need it?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks its real question: the second lesson of the ברייתא seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first lesson was needed. But the גמרא suspects we already know the second lesson, that any method is allowed, from another source. The next step names that source.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (this seems extra)
But (turns to the difficult part)

phrases.english: But "and dies" by any kind of death
that you are able to kill him with — why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא ״וָמֵת״ בְּכׇל מִיתָה שֶׁאַתָּה יָכוֹל לַהֲמִיתוֹ, לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the setup of step 11 to challenge the second lesson
steps.kashyaTarget: The lesson of 'ומת' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems we already know this from somewhere else, so the פסוק should not need to teach it.

steps.title: We already know it from a murderer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up its question: a ברייתא about a רוצח already teaches that if the normal method fails, any method may be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: It can be learned from a murderer, as a ברייתא teaches: 'The one who struck shall surely be put to death; he is a murderer.' From this alone I would only know to kill him with the death stated for him. From where do we know that if you cannot kill him with the death written for him, you may kill him with any death you can? The verse says 'shall surely be put to death', meaning in any way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where we already know the second lesson: from the law of a רוצח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The double wording 'מות יומת' teaches that a רוצח may be killed by any method if the normal one does not work. If that is true for a murderer, why would the burglar need his own פסוק for it? This makes the question of step 12 stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: A murderer
It can be learned (from another source)
He shall surely be put to death (double wording)
In any way, no matter what
The verse comes to teach

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an answer. It is proof that the question in step 12 is a real question. The answer comes in steps 14 through 16.

phrases.english: It can be learned from a murderer,
as it was taught in a ברייתא:
"The one who struck shall surely be put to death; he is a murderer" —
I would only know this
with the death stated for him.
And from where do we know that if you are not able
to kill him with the death written for him,
that you are allowed to kill him
with any death you are able to kill him with?
The verse says:
"shall surely be put to death" — in any way.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵרוֹצֵחַ נָפְקָא, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the question of step 12 by naming the source we already have
steps.raayaObject: That the 'ומת' lesson about the burglar is unnecessary
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא on 'מות יומת' (במדבר 35:21): a murderer may be killed in any way

steps.title: A murderer is different because the verse says 'מות יומת'
steps.stepSummary: The proof from רוצח is pushed away. There, the פסוק specifically says מות יומת, which allows any method of killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the verse says: 'He shall surely be put to death.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof it just brought from רוצח in step 13. It says that case has its own special word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13, the רוצח case seemed to show that any method of killing is always allowed, so ומת would be extra. Now the גמרא answers that the רוצח case only got that rule because its פסוק says מות יומת. So we cannot assume the same rule for a burglar without his own word.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
Because the verse says
He shall surely be put to death (the doubled wording teaches any method)

phrases.english: It is different there,
as the verse says: 'He shall surely be put to death.'
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק about a murderer, במדבר 35:21. The doubled wording is what allows any method of killing.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם, דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 13
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from רוצח that any method is always allowed
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רוצח rule comes from a special word, מות יומת, so it is not automatic for every case

steps.title: Why not learn the burglar from the murderer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we cannot learn from רוצח that any method of killing is allowed in every case where someone may be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us learn from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. Even if the rule comes from מות יומת, why not apply that rule to the burglar too?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah taught the rule once for רוצח, we could carry it over to other cases. Then the burglar would not need his own word ומת. So the question from step 12 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn from it

phrases.english: But let us learn from it!
phrases.notes: He means: learn from the murderer's case that any method is allowed for the burglar too.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנִיגְמַר מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the דחיה of step 14
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the burglar needs his own source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rule taught for one case should be carried over to similar cases, so ומת would be extra

steps.title: Two verses that come as one do not teach
steps.stepSummary: The rule appears in two places, רוצח and גואל הדם. Two verses that teach the same thing do not teach other cases, so the burglar needs ומת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the murderer and the blood redeemer are two verses that come as one, and any two verses that come as one do not teach.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we cannot learn from רוצח. The same rule appears in two places, and that tells us it does not spread to other cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rule were meant to apply everywhere, the Torah would only need to write it once. Writing it twice, for רוצח and for גואל הדם, shows that it is limited to those cases. That is why the ברייתא needed ומת to teach the rule for a burglar.

keyTerms.meaning: The blood redeemer, a relative of the victim who may kill the murderer
Two verses that teach the same thing
They do not teach other cases

steps.whatToRemember: When the Torah repeats the same rule in two places, that rule is not carried over to other cases. This is why the burglar needed his own word, ומת.
steps.whyThisMatters: שני כתובין הבאין כאחד אין מלמדין is a general rule of learning from פסוקים that appears all over ש״ס.

phrases.english: Because the murderer and the blood redeemer are
two verses that come as one,
and any two verses that come as one
do not teach.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה רוֹצֵחַ וְגוֹאֵל הַדָּם שְׁנֵי כְתוּבִין הַבָּאִין כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rule of learning from verses: a repeated rule stays limited
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Learn from רוצח that any method is allowed in every case, so ומת is extra
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is written twice, so it does not spread. The burglar needs ומת.

steps.title: The burglar's law applies anywhere he is found
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the law of בא במחתרת also applies if the burglar is found on the roof, in the yard, or in the enclosed area, because the פסוק says 'if the thief is found'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'Breaking in' means I only know breaking in. How do I know his roof, his yard and his enclosed area? The verse says 'if the thief is found', meaning anywhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about where the burglar law applies. It widens the law beyond a burglar who digs through the wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מחתרת alone would limit the law to breaking through a wall. The words 'ימצא הגנב' add that wherever the thief is found inside the owner's property, the same law applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Breaking in, by digging through a wall
His roof
His enclosed area behind the house
The verse teaches
In any place or case

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'Breaking in' –
I only know breaking in.
His roof, his yard and his enclosed area, from where do we know?
The verse says: 'If the thief is found' –
anywhere.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״מַחְתֶּרֶת״ – אֵין לִי אֶלָּא מַחְתֶּרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on the scope of the burglar law
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The burglar law applies wherever he is found on the owner's property

steps.title: Then why does the verse say 'breaking in'?
steps.stepSummary: Inside the ברייתא: if the law applies everywhere, why does the פסוק mention מחתרת at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does the verse say 'breaking in'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a question about its own conclusion. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once ימצא הגנב covers every place, the word מחתרת seems unnecessary. The ברייתא wants to know what that word is doing.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Why does the verse say

phrases.english: If so, why does the verse say 'breaking in'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״מַחְתֶּרֶת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word the previous step made seem unnecessary

steps.title: The verse speaks of the common case
steps.stepSummary: The word מחתרת is used only because most thieves are found breaking in. It does not limit the law.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because most thieves are found breaking in.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that the Torah just describes the usual situation. Breaking in is how thieves normally come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this ברייתא, מחתרת teaches no new law. The law is exactly the same everywhere. The Torah simply described the most common case.

keyTerms.meaning: Most thieves
Commonly found

phrases.english: Because most thieves are found breaking in.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרוֹב גַּנָּבִים מְצוּיִין בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 18
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מחתרת describes the common case and adds no new law

steps.title: A second ברייתא with the same opening
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא repeats the same teaching: the law applies on the roof, yard and enclosed area too. Then it asks the same question about why the verse says מחתרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in another ברייתא: 'Breaking in' means I only know breaking in. How do I know his roof, his yard and his enclosed area? The verse says 'if the thief is found', meaning anywhere. If so, why does the verse say 'breaking in'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that starts with exactly the same words as the first. This sets up a different answer about the word מחתרת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות agree that the law applies everywhere. They split only on what the word מחתרת adds. That difference comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: His yard

steps.confusionAlert: The first part of this ברייתא is the same, word for word, as step 17. Don't look for a difference there. The difference is only in the answer at the end.

phrases.english: It was taught in another ברייתא: 'Breaking in' –
I only know breaking in.
His roof, his yard and his enclosed area, from where do we know?
The verse says: 'If the thief is found' –
anywhere.
If so, why does the verse say 'breaking in'?

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״מַחְתֶּרֶת״ – אֵין לִי אֶלָּא מַחְתֶּרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא that repeats the setup of steps 17 and 18
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The burglar law applies wherever he is found on the owner's property

steps.title: Breaking in counts as his warning
steps.stepSummary: The second ברייתא says מחתרת teaches that breaking in itself serves as the burglar's התראה. One found elsewhere needs a real warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: His breaking in is his warning.
steps.whatsHappening: The second ברייתא gives its own answer: the word מחתרת teaches a real law about התראה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person may be killed only after a warning. Here, breaking in itself serves as that warning, so the owner does not need to warn him. A burglar found on the roof or in the yard without breaking in would still need a warning first, unlike in the first ברייתא, which saw no difference.

keyTerms.meaning: His breaking in
His warning, which is normally required before he may be killed

steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות agree the burglar law applies anywhere. They disagree about the word מחתרת. The first says it is just the common case. The second says breaking in takes the place of a warning.

phrases.english: His breaking in is his warning.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַחְתַּרְתּוֹ זוֹ הִיא הַתְרָאָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer from step 19 to the same question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מחתרת teaches that breaking in serves as the התראה

steps.title: רב הונא: even a child who chases to kill may be stopped with his life
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that a קטן הרודף may be killed to save the victim. The גמרא explains his reason: a רודף does not need התראה, so it makes no difference whether he is an adult or a child.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא says: if a child is chasing someone to kill him, you may save the victim even by killing the child. The reason is that he holds a רודף does not need a warning, so adults and children are the same.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a new rule: you may kill a child who is chasing someone to kill him. The גמרא then explains the reasoning behind his rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a קטן cannot be killed, since he is not punished for his actions and cannot really be warned. רב הונא says that does not matter here. Killing a רודף is not a punishment; it is a rescue. That is why no התראה is needed, and a child is the same as an adult.

keyTerms.meaning: A minor, a child who is not yet בר מצוה
A pursuer, someone chasing another person in order to kill him
The victim may be saved at the cost of the pursuer's life
A formal warning given before a sin
He holds, meaning this is his reasoning

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main question of the section: does a רודף need a warning before he may be killed?

phrases.english: Rav Huna says:
A minor who is pursuing [someone to kill him],
the victim may be saved with the pursuer's life.
He holds that a pursuer does not need a warning,

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא גָּדוֹל וְלָא שְׁנָא קָטָן.
phrases.english: there is no difference between an adult and a minor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: קָטָן הָרוֹדֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about רודף, after the discussion of התראה for בא במחתרת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A child who chases someone to kill him may be killed to save the victim, because a רודף needs no התראה.

steps.title: רב חסדא's challenge: a baby whose head has come out may not be harmed
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא brings a ברייתא: once the baby's head has come out during birth, we may not harm him to save the mother, because one life does not push aside another. But according to רב הונא, the baby should count as a רודף.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא challenged רב הונא: a ברייתא says that once a baby's head has come out, we do not touch him, because we do not push away one life for another. But why not? He is a רודף chasing his mother's life!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא attacks רב הונא's rule with a case of a dangerous birth. If even a child counts as a רודף, then a baby endangering his mother should also count as one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A baby has no intent at all, much like a קטן. If רב הונא is right that a child can be a רודף, the baby should be one too, and we should be allowed to save the mother. Yet the ברייתא forbids harming him, which seems to contradict רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: His head came out, meaning the baby is partly born
We do not push aside one life to save another life
But why?

steps.confusionAlert: Before the head comes out, the ברייתא allows saving the mother. The question is only about once the head has come out, when the baby already counts as a full person.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda raised an objection to Rav Huna:
Once his head has come out, we do not touch him,
phrases.notes: This is about a woman whose life is in danger while giving birth; 'his head' means the baby's.

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין דּוֹחִין נֶפֶשׁ מִפְּנֵי נֶפֶשׁ.
phrases.english: because we do not push aside one life for another life.
But why? He is a pursuer!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's rule from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that even a קטן counts as a רודף
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A baby endangering his mother should be a רודף too, yet the ברייתא forbids harming him once his head is out.

steps.title: The answer: in birth, the danger comes from Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that birth is different. The baby is not really chasing the mother; the danger comes from Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because Heaven is the one chasing her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא. It explains why the baby is not a רודף, even though a child can be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A child who chases someone is doing an act of chasing, even without full understanding. A baby being born is doing nothing at all; the danger is just a natural event sent from Heaven. So the baby is not a רודף, and רב הונא's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
From Heaven
They are chasing her

phrases.english: It is different there,
since she is being pursued from Heaven.
phrases.notes: He means the danger to the mother comes from nature, not from anything the baby is doing.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם, דְּמִשְּׁמַיָּא קָא רָדְפִי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's קשיא from step 23.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A baby endangering his mother is just like a child chasing someone, so he should be a רודף.
steps.terutzMaskana: The baby does no act of chasing; Heaven causes the danger, so he is not a רודף. A child who actually chases is one.

steps.title: A suggested proof for רב הונא from a ברייתא about warning a pursuer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a ברייתא supports רב הונא. The ברייתא says we tell the רודף that the victim is a Jew and quote the פסוק, and the Torah says to save one person's blood with the other's. It does not say the רודף must accept the warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this supports him? If a רודף was chasing someone to kill him, we tell him: 'See, he is a Jew and a member of the covenant, and the Torah said, Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed.' The Torah said: save the blood of this one with the blood of that one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to bring support for רב הונא's idea that a רודף needs no real התראה. It quotes a ברייתא about what we say to a pursuer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a formal התראה needs the sinner to show he heard and accepted it. This ברייתא only says we speak to the רודף and then allows saving the victim. It does not require the רודף to answer, so it seems a full התראה is not needed, as רב הונא said.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this supports him?
A member of the covenant
Whoever sheds the blood of man
Save!

phrases.english: Shall we say that this supports him:
A pursuer who was pursuing
after another person to kill him,
we say to him:
See that he is a Jew
and he is a member of the covenant,
and the Torah said:
"Whoever sheds the blood of man,
by man shall his blood be shed."
The Torah said:

phrases.aramaic: הַצֵּל דָּמוֹ שֶׁל זֶה בְּדָמוֹ שֶׁל זֶה.
phrases.english: Save the blood of this one with the blood of that one.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the person being chased; 'that one' is the chaser.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After answering רב חסדא's challenge in step 24, the גמרא now tries to find a ברייתא that supports רב הונא's ruling from step 22.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's view that a רודף needs no התראה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that allows saving the victim without requiring the רודף to accept the warning

steps.title: The proof is rejected: the ברייתא follows רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof. The ברייתא may follow רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, who holds that a חבר needs no התראה, since a warning is only meant to tell accidental from deliberate sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא follows רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה. As it was taught: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says, a חבר does not need a warning, because a warning is only given to tell the difference between someone who sinned by accident and someone who sinned on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 25. It says the ברייתא matches only one opinion, so it cannot prove the הלכה for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה holds that the only point of התראה is to show the sinner acted on purpose. A רודף clearly acts on purpose, so by his view no warning is needed. But the חכמים who argue with him require התראה even for a חבר, so they might require it for a רודף too, and the ברייתא proves nothing for רב הונא according to them.

keyTerms.meaning: A person learned in Torah law who surely knows the הלכה
Someone who sins by accident
Someone who sins on purpose
To tell apart

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא says a רודף, even a child, needs no warning. The baby in birth is not a רודף because the danger is from Heaven. The ברייתא about warning a רודף cannot prove רב הונא's view, because it may follow only רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying רב הונא is wrong. It only says this ברייתא is not a strong enough proof for him.

phrases.aramaic: הָהִיא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא,
phrases.english: That one follows Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the ברייתא just quoted about warning the pursuer.

phrases.english: as it was taught:
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says:
A learned person does not need a warning,
because a warning was given only
to tell apart one who sins by accident from one who sins on purpose.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the attempted proof from step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the ברייתא is rejected; רב הונא's ruling itself stays in place.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may reflect only רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's view that someone who clearly acts on purpose needs no warning, which the חכמים do not accept.

steps.title: A ברייתא that seems to require a warning for a רודף
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: we warn the רודף. If he does not accept the warning he is פטור, and if he accepts it he is חייב. This suggests a רודף needs התראה, which goes against רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if a רודף was chasing someone to kill him, we tell him, 'Know that this is a Jew and a member of the covenant, and the Torah says: whoever sheds a man's blood, his blood shall be shed.' If he answers, 'I know it is so,' he is פטור. If he answers, 'I am doing it on that condition,' he is חייב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to prove a רודף needs a warning, and he has to accept it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a רודף can only be killed after he hears a warning and accepts it, then a קטן cannot be killed, because a child's acceptance means nothing. So this ברייתא goes against רב הונא's ruling in Step 22, which allowed killing a קטן הרודף because a רודף needs no warning.

keyTerms.meaning: A member of the covenant, meaning a Jew
Exempt; here it means he may not be killed
Liable; here it means he may be killed
On that condition; he knows the punishment and does it anyway

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two answers. 'I know it is so' sounds like he understood, but it is NOT accepting the warning, so he is פטור. Only 'I am doing it on that condition' counts as accepting it.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: רוֹדֵף שֶׁהָיָה רוֹדֵף אַחַר חֲבֵירוֹ לְהוֹרְגוֹ,
phrases.english: A pursuer who was chasing after another person to kill him,
we say to him:
See that he is a Jew
and he is a member of the covenant,
and the Torah said:
"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed."

phrases.aramaic: אִם אָמַר: יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁהוּא כֵּן – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: If he said: I know that it is so, he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: עַל מְנָת כֵּן אֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: If he said: I am doing it on that condition, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof for רב הונא was pushed off in Step 26, the גמרא now brings a source that seems to prove the opposite.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule (Step 22) that a רודף needs no התראה, so even a קטן הרודף may be killed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires a warning and the רודף's acceptance before he is חייב. A קטן cannot accept a warning, so he should not be killed.

steps.title: The warning is only for bringing him to court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a bystander who cannot stop the רודף, for example because a river is between them. He wants to bring the רודף to בית דין, and a בית דין needs התראה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only needed when they stand on two sides of a river, so the bystander cannot save the victim. What can he do? He wants to bring the רודף to בית דין, and a בית דין needs a warning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the ברייתא to a case where nobody can stop the רודף on the spot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate things: killing a רודף on the spot to save the victim, and a בית דין punishing a killer later. The ברייתא's warning is only for the second. Saving a victim right then still needs no warning, so רב הונא's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for; the גמרא limits a source to a specific case
The sides of a river
To save him
Court

steps.whyThisMatters: It separates stopping a רודף now, which needs no warning, from a בית דין's punishment later, which does need a warning.

phrases.english: It is only needed
where they are standing on two sides of a river,
phrases.notes: The person giving the warning is on one side, and the רודף is on the other side.

phrases.english: so that he cannot save him.
What is there for him to do?
He wants to bring him to court.
And a court requires a warning.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 27 by narrowing the ברייתא to a specific case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ברייתא is about punishment in בית דין, not about saving the victim
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that any רודף must be warned before he may be killed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning is only for a בית דין's punishment, when the bystander cannot save the victim. Killing a רודף to save the victim needs no warning.

steps.title: רב הונא follows the תנא of מחתרת
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: רב הונא can say he follows the תנא of מחתרת, who holds that breaking in is itself the warning. In the same way, the chasing itself is the רודף's warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: רב הונא could tell you, 'I hold like the תנא of the break-in, who says that his breaking in is his warning.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer. רב הונא admits the ברייתא disagrees with him, but says he follows a different תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ברייתא is not explained away. Instead, it is a מחלוקת תנאים. The תנא of מחתרת says the dangerous act counts as the warning. So a רודף, even a קטן, needs no separate warning.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say; it introduces a second, different answer
A sage from the time of the משנה
Breaking in; the case of a burglar who digs into a house

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's rule survives in two ways: (1) the ברייתא's warning is only for a בית דין's punishment, or (2) רב הונא follows the תנא of מחתרת, who says the act itself is the warning.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
Rav Huna could say to you:
I said my ruling like the tanna of the break-in,
who said: his breaking in is his warning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אָמַר לְךָ רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the קשיא of Step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מחלוקת תנאים: רב הונא follows a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא requiring a warning seemed to be the only view, so it would disprove רב הונא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא follows the תנא of מחתרת, who holds that the dangerous act itself is the warning. So a רודף, even a קטן, needs no separate warning.
